Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-04-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Lumina CTO), Evan Cole (Lumina Head of SRE), Dr. Lena Brooks (Lumina Head of ML)
Recording ID: ff-20260409-lumina-001

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- Lumina is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private options for a clinical-assist product. Main concerns: multi-region failover, graceful degradation, recovery time objectives and auditability.
- They want a pilot to validate fallback to smaller quantized models and regional routing under load.
- Security/regulatory constraints: PHI handling, data residency, SSO + audit logs.

Topics: redundancy topology, model fallbacks, SLA expectations, VPC/private deployment, observability and audit logs, pilot scope.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, I'm Maya, AE, with Redwood Inference. Diego will cover technical bits.
[00:12] Priya: Hi, Priya Shah here, CTO at Lumina Health. We've got Evan, our SRE lead, and Lena from ML.
[00:19] Evan: Hey.
[00:20] Lena: Hello.
[00:22] Diego: Diego Ramos, solutions engineer. We'll try to keep this practical and leave time for Qs.

[01:05] Maya: Goal for today - understand failure modes you care about, what counts as acceptable degradation, and whether Hosted / Dedicated / Private fits those needs. We'll surface fallback patterns and then map a pilot.

[02:15] Priya: Quick context: Lumina runs a clinical decision assist that enriches notes and flags contradictions. It's latency sensitive for clinician workflow - ideally sub 400ms p95 for short prompts, but for some long summarization flows we accept higher. We also must not persist PHI outside approved regions.

[03:02] Evan: Our ops constraints: SLA to clinicians is 99.9% uptime during business hours, and an SLO error budget we can't blow. If region X has an outage we need automated failover within a couple minutes and deterministic behavior - we can't have clinicians get wildly different model outputs.

[03:38] Diego: Good, that's helpful. Quick question on traffic shape - is it spiky? steady?
[03:45] Evan: Very spiky - big bursts at shift changes and end-of-day charting. Baseline ~40 rps, peaks up to 600 rps for short period.

[04:12] Lena: Also model side - we are sensitive to model drift. We want to ensure fallback models don't produce unsafe hallucinations; quality regression windows must be small.

[04:35] Maya: Right. So there are several levers: multi-region routing, model variant fallback (e.g., full model -> quantized variant -> small family model) and degraded feature sets (disable long context generation, fall back to cached responses). We'll walk through options.

[05:20] Diego: First topology: Active-active multi-region hosted. Requests route to nearest region; when a region detects degraded capacity it reroutes to a second region. That gives low RTO but you need data residency handling - e.g., some requests must stay in-region.

[06:02] Priya: For PHI, our legal says certain patient records must not leave EU. We have mixed footprint - US+EU. So any cross-region fallback needs to be controlled per tenancy or per dataset.

[06:27] Diego: We can do routing policy by project or dataset tag. For in-region only traffic, you still get fallback within the same region to a different availability zone or to a dedicated pool.

[06:45] Evan: What happens for capacity exhaustion? If the primary region is out of GPU capacity, can Redwood warm up instances in another region? Cold spin up will add minutes.

[07:03] Diego: Correct — cold starts are minutes. We support warm standby and reserved capacity (Dedicated) for predictable throughput. Dedicated in two regions or a hybrid: Dedicated primary + Hosted failover. That gives you guaranteed baseline and a fallback path.

[07:40] Priya: Cost tradeoffs are huge there. Dedicated double-region is expensive. We need to quantify expected incremental cost vs risk.

[08:05] Maya: Agreed. For the pilot, we typically recommend a small dedicated pool sized to handle p50 traffic in each region and a hosted failover for spikes; that reduces most mission-critical risk without a full double-reserved footprint. We'll send numbers.

[08:35] Lena: About model fallbacks — can we define deterministic fallback rules? For example: full Florence-13B -> quantized Florence-13B-8bit -> Florence-4B -> cached reply. We need to know regression deltas and have a rollback switch.

[09:10] Diego: Yes. Our runtime supports model-tiering with automatic kernel/quant selection. Fallback rules are policy-driven and can be evaluated per-request. You can tie a quality threshold to trigger fallback; Redwood Optimize can flag regressions against your prompt suite.

[09:42] Priya: How are prompts and KV caches handled across fallback? If we switch model family mid-session, could we lose context?

[10:00] Diego: Good call. KV cache format differs across families; when we fallback to a different architecture we may need to restart the session. We support prefix caching — retaining precomputed embeddings or summaries — to reduce recompute. But full token-level KV carryover between quantized variants is supported for compatible runtimes; for different architectures it's a session restart with best-effort stitching.

[10:40] Evan: That stitching risk is a concern for clinical dialog — if context is lost we might get inconsistent advice. Can we test that in pilot?

[10:51] Maya: Absolutely. Pilot runbook will include fallbacks and repeatability tests. We'll define acceptance criteria with you.

[11:25] Priya: On SLA, Redwood advertises multi-tier SLAs. For Hosted, what is typical p95 latency SLO?

[11:36] Diego: For hosted inference on our standard models we typically aim for sub-250ms p95 for short prompts on standard instance sizes in low contention, but that varies by model and seq length. For strict SLOs and guaranteed capacity, Dedicated comes with contractual latency/uptime commitments.

[12:05] Priya: We need 99.9% during business hours, and RTO under 5 minutes for failover. Can Redwood contract to that for Dedicated?

[12:18] Maya: Yes, Dedicated contracts can include those SLOs; we'll include specifics in the commercial. For hosted we can offer SLOs for higher tiers though not always contractual.

[12:39] Evan: Observability and auditing are key. We need token-level cost breakdowns, per-request tracing, and immutable audit logs for compliance. Does Redwood provide HSM/KMS integration and tamper-evident audit trails?

[12:58] Diego: KMS/HSM integrations are supported in Private and Dedicated; Hosted supports customer-managed keys for some enterprise tiers. Audit logs with append-only behavior are in our private deployment and enterprise log add-on. We'll share the security pack.

[13:27] Lena: How about model provenance? We need to know which model variant generated an output and the exact model commit.

[13:35] Diego: Each response includes metadata: model id, flavor, quantization, and commit hash. We persist that in request logs for traces and can surface via Redwood Console.

[14:05] Priya: Let's talk degraded modes. Suppose a region loses GPU nodes: options are redirect to other region, fall back to smaller model, or serve cached answers. Which path is least risky?

[14:25] Diego: It depends on the workflow. For single-turn quick checks, redirect to another region tends to preserve model parity. For long-running context-heavy flows, a quantized variant might maintain better user experience if locality is required. Cached answers are safest for deterministic outputs but can cause staleness.

[15:10] Evan: On consistency: when we redirect across regions, outputs could differ slightly. Clinicians might notice different phrasing. Can we pin to a canonical model family to reduce variance?

[15:25] Maya: You can pin to the same model family/version in both regions; Redwood's model catalog supports version pinning and rollout policies so you can ensure parity.

[16:00] Priya: What about fail-open vs fail-closed behavior? For some endpoints we prefer to fail closed (return an error) rather than risk giving a wrong suggestion.

[16:12] Diego: Policies are configurable per route. You can set failure modes: fail-open with degraded model, fail-closed (503), or degrade feature set. We'll test each in pilot with your acceptance tests.

[16:40] Lena: Regarding benchmarking: how can we reproduce your hosted latency numbers? We want a runbook to hit same seq lengths, batch patterns, and KV warm states.

[16:58] Diego: We'll give a benchmark harness and recommended prompts. For pilots we can run side-by-side A/B comparisons: your self-hosted baseline vs Redwood hosted/dedicated, and collect p95, p99, cost per token, and regression on labeled prompts.

[17:30] Evan: Also need to test network partitions, long tail latency, and partial degradation scenarios. We want to codify runbook steps for incident response.

[17:45] Maya: We'll draft a playbook: detection, automatic reroute steps, manual escalation, and rollback. Diego will include example incident playbooks.

[18:05] Priya: One legal/security nuance - we can't have logs containing raw PHI in third-party systems unless encrypted and auditable. How do you handle transient storage?

[18:22] Diego: Redwood supports redaction hooks and request-level transformations before logs are persisted. For private/Dedicated we can keep logs inside your VPC. We'll include the data flow diagram in the security docs.

[19:10] Evan: For Private deployment, what's the lift? Are we talking about a customer-managed control plane or full on-prem?

[19:25] Diego: Private has two flavors: VPC-hosted control plane with customer-managed networking and a packaged on-prem install for air-gapped environments. VPC option is fastest to stand up; on-prem takes more time and integration with your ops tooling.

[19:50] Priya: Timeline constraints: we need a pilot in 4–6 weeks. Is that doable?

[19:58] Maya: Yes, for a scoped pilot focusing on fallbacks and model parity we can do 4–6 weeks. We'll propose a minimal dedicated pool plus hosted failover for the pilot.

[20:12] Lena: A couple of detailed Qs - can we run canary rollouts and A/B test fallback behavior with traffic split rules?

[20:23] Diego: Yes, Redwood supports canary and traffic-splitting with rollout policies. You can route a percent of users to fallback or to a new model and monitor quality metrics.

[20:45] Priya: If we do a rollback, how quick is model rollback?

[20:52] Diego: Model rollback within a region is typically seconds to a minute if versions are pre-warmed; if you need to load a new artifact cold it's minutes. That's why we recommend pre-warmed versions for critical paths.

[21:20] Evan: About pricing and cost predictability - we want a model to estimate burst cost if we have to failover to hosted from dedicated.

[21:32] Maya: We'll provide a cost table and scenarios. Typical pilot includes baseline committed capacity and a capped burst spend budget to bound risk.

[22:05] Priya: On the security front, we need SOC 2 Type II, penetration test reports, and our vendor questionnaire answered.

[22:15] Maya: We'll attach SOC 2 and the security questionnaire. Diego will follow up with network diagrams.

[22:40] Lena: Operational question - how are alerts surfaced? PagerDuty integration? Slack?

[22:48] Diego: Both. We have webhook integrations, Datadog, PagerDuty, and Slack. Console has per-route alerting and anomaly detection.

[23:15] Priya: One more thing - can we run a small chaos test during pilot? Simulate AZ failure and observe behavior.

[23:26] Diego: Absolutely. We'll include chaos scenarios in the pilot runbook: AZ kill, network partition, cold-start recovery, quantized fallback, and cross-region routing.

[24:00] (Cross talk)
[24:05] Evan: Ok, good.
[24:07] Priya: Sounds solid.

[24:20] Maya: Quick recap / next steps - we'll send a pilot runbook and cost estimate, security docs, and schedule a deep-dive next week. Any final blockers?

[24:33] Priya: We need to vet the cost internally but otherwise good. We'll confirm the deep-dive attendees.

[24:45] Lena: Please include a sample set of prompts we should use to check hallucination/regression.

[24:56] Maya: We'll include that.

[25:10] Diego: I'll also prepare a short test harness for model-fallback tests.

[25:18] Evan: And we'll pull our p95/p99 metrics and traffic traces.

[25:25] Maya: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with materials and a proposed pilot timeline.
